reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
clinicalPearls: Arises from a variant of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (HPD) in the tyrosine degradation pathway, producing an abnormal reactive intermediate rather than complete enzyme loss
Named for the excretion of hawkinsin, a cyclic sulphur-containing amino acid formed from a reactive epoxide intermediate that conjugates with glutathione
Uniquely among these disorders it is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, unlike most tyrosine pathway defects
Symptomatic infants may present around weaning with failure to thrive, metabolic acidosis, and fine hair, often improving with age
Urine may also contain 4-hydroxycyclohexylacetic acid, and there can be evidence of glutathione depletion from ongoing conjugation of the reactive intermediate
Many individuals become asymptomatic after infancy, and management in symptomatic infants centres on tyrosine/phenylalanine dietary moderation and ascorbic acid support
It should be distinguished from the hepatorenal and oculocutaneous tyrosinaemias
reference.pathophysiology: In the tyrosine degradation pathway, 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase normally converts 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate to homogentisate. In hawkinsinuria, a variant enzyme carries out an incomplete reaction that releases a reactive epoxide-like intermediate. This intermediate is conjugated with glutathione to form the characteristic metabolite hawkinsin, and its ongoing production can deplete glutathione and generate related metabolites such as 4-hydroxycyclohexylacetic acid. The reactive intermediate and glutathione consumption are thought to underlie the transient infantile symptoms, which typically remit as the child grows.
additionalDifferentials: Tyrosinaemia type I (hepatorenal, fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency)
Tyrosinaemia type II (oculocutaneous, tyrosine aminotransferase deficiency)
Other causes of infantile failure to thrive with metabolic acidosis
Alkaptonuria (a distal defect in the same pathway)
Dietary or hepatic causes of tyrosine elevation
additionalInvestigations: Urine organic acids identifying hawkinsin and 4-hydroxycyclohexylacetic acid
Quantitative plasma amino acids including tyrosine
Assessment of acid-base status in symptomatic infants
Molecular analysis of the HPD gene
Family studies consistent with dominant inheritance
Markers of glutathione status where available
redFlags: Failure to thrive with metabolic acidosis in an infant requiring nutritional intervention
Features suggesting hepatorenal tyrosinaemia type I, which is far more serious
Persistent symptoms beyond infancy, prompting reassessment
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally good; symptomatic infants usually improve after weaning and many become asymptomatic in later childhood and adulthood. Serious sequelae are uncommon.
pitfalls: Confusing it with the far more dangerous tyrosinaemia type I
Overlooking the unusual autosomal dominant inheritance
Missing the diagnosis because hawkinsin is not a routinely named metabolite
Failing to support nutrition and ascorbate status during symptomatic infancy

Nyhan, Atlas of Inherited Metabolic Diseases
management: Moderate dietary tyrosine and phenylalanine intake in symptomatic infants to reduce flux through the defective pathway
Supplement with ascorbic acid to support residual enzyme function and limit the reactive intermediate
Maintain adequate nutrition and provide additional support around weaning, when symptoms typically appear
Correct metabolic acidosis and manage failure to thrive with supportive care
Monitor growth, acid-base status, and urinary metabolites, reassuring that symptoms usually remit with age
Offer genetic counselling and family studies given autosomal dominant HPD inheritance
